strengths: The experimental protocol is systematic and reasonably well-controlled: per-latent threshold calibration, relevance/concreteness filters on steering latents, a no-steering baseline (0/7,892 multi-attempt responses), and a matched random-ablation control. The ablation-with-control design is a sensible way to probe causal relevance.

Judge robustness is handled better than in many papers: five judges from different providers are compared, with reported 90-96% agreement on multi-attempt detection and consistent relative rankings. The paper is transparent that stratified sampling inflates absolute ESR values.

The limitations section is unusually honest, explicitly flagging the single-layer SAE constraint, the 25% (partial) ablation effect, the prompt-set reuse for both OTD identification and evaluation, and the fact that the phenomenon may be Llama-specific.

The framing of ESR and its dual-use implications for alignment (resistance to adversarial steering vs. interference with beneficial steering) is a thought-provoking angle that could motivate follow-up work.
Fine-tuning and meta-prompting experiments are a reasonable attempt to establish controllability, and the dissociation between attempt frequency and attempt success is an interesting observation.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim of 'dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits' is not well-supported. By the authors' own admission, roughly half of the 26 'off-topic detector' latents show the opposite or null pattern (Table 2 has many negative Cohen's d values), and the surviving labels ('Auxiliary verbs forming perfect tenses,' 'Syntactical sugar in programming languages,' 'End of message token in chat format,' 'System header temporal context markers') look like generic formatting/syntactic features that differ between matched and shuffled pairs for trivial reasons, not coherence-monitoring features. Contrastive search on matched vs. shuffled pairs is a weak basis for labeling these as off-topic detectors.

The cross-model comparison—one of the paper's headline claims ('only Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial ESR')—is confounded by post-hoc, outcome-based layer selection. The authors selected layer 33 for Llama-3.3-70B (SAE trained on layer 50) because it 'produced higher-quality results,' and layer 22 for Gemma-2-27B because it showed 'higher ESR incidence.' Selecting the layer that maximizes the target outcome per model makes the between-model differences difficult to interpret. Additional confounds (Goodfire vs. GemmaScope SAEs, pretrained vs. instruction-tuned SAE training, family/architecture/scale) mean the scale claim is essentially untestable with this design.

The effect sizes are very small. ESR is 3.8% and multi-attempt 7.4% for the one model that 'shows' the effect; the improvement-rate statistics for the smaller models rest on a handful of episodes (e.g., n=5 for Gemma-2-2B, acknowledged by the authors). A phenomenon defined by ~3% of responses is a fragile basis for strong mechanistic conclusions.

The meta-prompting result is close to tautological: the winning prompt ('If you notice yourself going off-topic, stop and force yourself to get back on track') explicitly instructs the model to produce self-correction language, and the metric (multi-attempt rate) is defined by detecting that same language. An increase under this prompt is largely a restatement of the instruction, not evidence about latent self-monitoring circuits. Selecting the best-performing prompt variant among several further weakens this.

The interpretation of surface self-correction phrases as 'internal monitoring' is over-reaching. A more parsimonious explanation—that off-topic content under steering elicits continuation patterns associated with correction/backtracking tokens learned in-context—is not ruled out, and the fine-tuning result (behavior inducible, effectiveness not) is arguably more consistent with that mundane account than with a dedicated monitoring circuit.

The 25-27% ablation reduction is modest, and an alternative explanation (that the ablated latents carry part of the steering signal or generic content needed for the recovery behavior) is not excluded. The random-ablation control is a step in the right direction but does not fully establish specificity to 'monitoring.'

Methodological artifacts are insufficiently addressed: the repetition penalty used during generation could itself interact with the self-correction behavior, and the judge's segmentation depends entirely on detecting explicit verbal markers, so 'implicit' monitoring (if any) is invisible and the metrics measure a narrow surface behavior.

strengths: Identifies an interesting and under-explored phenomenon (endogenous mid-generation recovery under activation steering) that is potentially relevant to interpretability and AI-safety debates about steering-based interventions.

The empirical protocol is relatively large-scale (~5,000 trials per model) and includes useful controls: a no-steering baseline yielding 0 multi-attempt responses across 7,892 trials, and a random-latent ablation control matched on activation frequency/magnitude, which partially addresses specificity concerns.
Cross-judge validation across five judge models from different providers shows consistent model rankings, lending some robustness to the behavioral comparison.

The limitations section is candid, explicitly acknowledging that scale/architecture/training cannot be disentangled, that only single-layer SAEs are used, that the same prompt set is used for latent identification and evaluation, and that the ablation effect is only partial.
weaknesses: Central mechanistic claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper concludes that a set of latents forms 'dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits,' yet by its own Table 2 roughly half of the 26 'off-topic detector' latents have near-zero or negative effect sizes, and the labels (e.g., 'Document structure and formatting tokens,' 'Auxiliary verbs forming perfect tenses,' 'End of message token in chat format') do not plausibly correspond to coherence monitoring. A group ablation of 26 heterogeneous latents cannot license the 'off-topic detector circuit' interpretation.

The cross-model comparison is heavily confounded and cannot support the scale framing used throughout. Models use different SAEs (Goodfire vs. GemmaScope), different layers and depths (41.3% for Llama-3.3-70B vs. 47.8-61.9% for others), and GemmaScope SAEs trained on pretrained rather than instruction-tuned models. The paper admits it cannot isolate scale/architecture/training, yet repeatedly asserts 'effects scaling by model size'; the apparent scaling rests on a single outlier (Llama-3.3-70B), and within Gemma the trend is nearly flat (0.1% -> 1.0% -> 1.1%).

Layer selection is post hoc and outcome-driven ('selected layer 22 based on higher ESR incidence'; layer 33 'produced higher-quality results with more interpretable ESR behavior'), raising a garden-of-forking-paths concern that inflates the headline effect for the largest model.

The sequential activation analysis (Figure 7; Appendix A.4) is largely circular: the latents were selected precisely because they activate more strongly on off-topic content, so the reported '4.4x higher during off-topic content' finding mostly restates the selection criterion rather than independently validating a monitoring mechanism.

Absolute effect sizes are small and the ablation result is marginal. ESR drops only from 3.8% to 2.8% and multi-attempt from 7.4% to 5.5%, with 95% CIs that barely separate; clamping 26 latents to zero simultaneously is a large, non-specific intervention whose attribution to 'off-topic detection' remains uncertain.

Reproducibility is undermined by judge inconsistency: Section 2.1 states the judge is Claude 4.5 Haiku, while Appendix A.2.2 refers to 'our original Claude 4.5 Sonnet judge.' Which judge produced the primary results is unclear.

The fine-tuning result does not support the stated conclusion. The authors themselves list five interpretations, including a floor effect and the possibility that the base model 'already corrects as effectively as possible,' which would make the attempt/success dissociation uninformative; nevertheless the paper concludes that 'genuine self-monitoring may require mechanisms beyond behavioral imitation.'

Threshold calibration is arbitrary and unstable: the threshold is defined as the boost yielding an average judge score of 30/100, while first-attempt scores are acknowledged to be bimodal and high-variance; the applied repetition penalty of 1.1 may also confound steering-induced self-correction.

Presentation and reference quality are weak (e.g., 'Grattafori' for Grattafiori; 'Towards monoseismicity'/'monoseimantic-features' for monosemanticity; Hu et al. cited as 2016 but dated 2022; inconsistent Graziano citations), which reduces confidence in the overall care of the work.

The core conceptual claim that ESR reflects 'self-monitoring' or 'internal consistency checking' is not distinguished from a simpler behavioral account (RLHF-induced production of self-correction phrases), and the paper's own fine-tuning result is consistent with the behavioral-imitation explanation for smaller models.

strengths: Identifies and systematically characterizes an interesting and under-explored phenomenon (Endogenous Steering Resistance), with a clear operationalization via two complementary metrics (multi-attempt rate and ESR rate).

Strong experimental hygiene: a no-steering baseline showing 0/7,892 self-corrections, a matched random-latent ablation control that moves in the opposite direction (3.8%→4.2%), and cross-judge validation with five judges from different providers all agreeing on the relative model ranking.
Honest, detailed limitations section that flags the scale/architecture/training confound, the partial nature of the ablation effect, and the fact that 'off-topic detector' is a functional label.

Good reproducibility: public models (Llama-3, Gemma-2) and public SAEs (GemmaScope, Goodfire), with detailed appendices giving judge prompts, filtering procedures, threshold calibration, and fine-tuning hyperparameters.

The fine-tuning dissociation (attempt frequency is trainable while correction effectiveness is not) is a genuinely informative negative result with plausible implications for whether self-monitoring can be imitated behaviorally.
Thoughtful dual-use discussion of the alignment implications: ESR as protection against adversarial steering vs. interference with beneficial safety interventions like ITI/RepE.
weaknesses: Effect sizes are very small (best-model ESR 3.8%, multi-attempt 7.4%; all other models below 1%), so essentially every claim rests on rare events, and the smaller-model improvement statistics are based on a handful of episodes (e.g., n=5 for Gemma-2-2B, which the paper itself notes may be unreliable).

The central mechanistic claim of 'dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits' is weakly supported: the paper's own Table 2 shows roughly half of the 26 'off-topic detector' latents have near-zero or negative effect sizes, and labels such as 'Auxiliary verbs forming perfect tenses' and 'Document structure and formatting tokens' do not read as off-topic detectors, so the ablated set is heterogeneous and the functional interpretation is shaky.

The cross-model comparison is confounded. Gemma SAEs were trained on pretrained (not instruction-tuned) models while the Llama SAEs target instruction-tuned models, and Llama-3.3-70B is steered at layer 33 even though the SAE was trained on layer 50. The headline claim that 'only Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial ESR' may therefore partly reflect SAE/steering-target mismatch rather than a genuine model-capability difference.

Post-hoc layer selection is a garden-of-forking-paths concern: the authors explicitly chose layer 33 for 70B and layer 22 for Gemma-2-27B because they yielded the most ESR, and acknowledge this could bias results — yet the headline cross-model contrast depends on exactly this choice.

The scale interpretation is not identifiable: only 5 models across 2 families, each with family-specific SAEs, so the asserted 'scaling by model size' cannot be disentangled from architecture or training, as the authors concede.

The definition of ESR (rate at which the model both self-corrects and improves) is close to tautological with the measured behavior, and 'improvement' depends on subjective judge scoring with a somewhat arbitrary calibration target (first-attempt score of 30/100).

The ablation only reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25% (7.4%→5.5%); the paper itself states this implies additional mechanisms, so the identified latents are not shown to be 'the' consistency-checking circuit, undercutting the strong framing in the abstract/intro.

The fine-tuning result is inconclusive — the authors enumerate five alternative interpretations, and 'improvement rate stays flat' is equally consistent with the model simply learning surface self-correction phrases without any underlying monitoring.

Minor but pervasive citation/proofing errors (e.g., 'Grattafori et al., 2024' for Llama 3, the Graziano & Kastner reference listed as 'Graziano et al., 2021', the Bricken URL 'monoseismicity') suggest insufficient care in preparing the manuscript.

strengths: Introduces a novel and potentially important phenomenon: mid-generation recovery from activation steering, with implications for interpretability and AI safety.

Extensive experimental suite across five models, including a no-steering baseline (0/7,892), cross-judge validation (five judges), Wikipedia-derived steering vectors, held-out prompts, random-latent ablation, prefilling control, matched-prefix experiment, and fine-tuning sweep.
The prefilling control provides a useful dissociation between text-conditioned detection (restart) and correction quality, showing that steering impairs correction success.

The matched-prefix experiment offers evidence that natural post-correction text improves sustained on-topic generation beyond a length-matched on-topic prefix, suggesting the corrective event does non-trivial work.

Honest and detailed limitations section; cautious interpretation; revised terminology to 'self-correction-associated' latents; negative results reported (holistic judge failure, fine-tuning does not improve success).

Good reproducibility details: judge prompts, steering equations, threshold calibration, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and prompt sets are provided; code is mentioned (though the URL is missing in the PDF).
Ethical impact statement and discussion of dual-use safety implications.
weaknesses: The 'endogenous' framing is not supported by the evidence: the prefilling control shows an unsteered model given off-topic text self-corrects more often (7–13.5%) and more successfully (~95%) than the steered model (2–3%, ~50%), indicating steering impairs self-correction rather than inducing endogenous resistance. The residual sustained resistance is not isolated from richer text conditioning.

Post-hoc layer selection biases results: for Llama-3.3-70B, steering is applied at layer 33 despite the SAE being trained on layer 50; for Gemma-2-27B, layer 22 was chosen because it yielded higher ESR incidence. This cherry-picking likely inflates effect sizes and confounds cross-model comparisons.

Cross-model comparison is confounded by different SAE sources (Goodfire vs. GemmaScope), some SAEs trained on pretrained rather than instruction-tuned models, different relative depths, and per-model best-layer selection. The claim that only the largest model shows substantial ESR cannot be attributed to scale, architecture, or training.

Mechanistic identification is weak: the 26 latents are heterogeneous, about half have negative effect size, and ablating both positive and negative subsets reduces ESR, undermining a clean off-topic detector interpretation. Ablation reduces ESR only from 3.8% to 2.8% (~27%), with random ablation within confidence intervals.

The metric captures only explicit verbal restarts; implicit recovery is unmeasured. The holistic judge attempted to broaden this but failed validation (systematically overscoring gradual shifts), leaving the broader phenomenon unquantified.
Fine-tuning and meta-prompting increase attempts but not correction success, so the 'enhancement' is superficial and the practical safety benefit remains speculative.

The manuscript contains references to 'reviewer feedback' and 'during the rebuttal period' in the main text, violating double-blind norms and indicating prior review history; the code URL in the abstract is missing.

Safety implications are speculative and untested with safety-relevant steering (e.g., harmful content, honesty), and the steering paradigm is limited to additive residual-stream interventions at a single layer.
Some statistical concerns: small n for some multi-attempt statistics (e.g., Gemma-2-2B n=5), held-out prompt set n=239, and wide confidence intervals in several ablation conditions.

strengths: Addresses an interesting and timely question: whether LLMs can detect and recover from activation-space perturbations, with implications for interpretability and safety.

Provides a systematic experimental protocol across five models, using SAE-based steering, judge scoring, and multiple controls (no-steering baseline, prefilling, matched-prefix, random-latent ablation, held-out prompts, Wikipedia-derived vectors, cross-judge validation).

The paper is generally honest about limitations: it distinguishes detection from sustained resistance, acknowledges noisy auto-generated labels and the narrow explicit-restart metric, and refrains from claiming a clean monitoring circuit.

Some useful dissociations are reported: fine-tuning induces more self-correction attempts without improving success; meta-prompting primarily increases attempts; prefilling shows restarts are text-conditioned. These negative/dissociative results may inform future work.
Appendices provide substantial detail (judge prompts, hyperparameters, prompt lists, ablation statistics), and the authors state that code is available.
The cross-judge analysis, while limited, supports that the relative ranking of Llama-3.3-70B is not solely an artifact of one judge.
weaknesses: The central 'endogenous steering resistance' claim is not well supported. The headline explicit ESR rate is only 3.8% in Llama-3.3-70B, and smaller models are below 1% with tiny multi-attempt counts (e.g., n=5 for Gemma-2-2B); scale, architecture, and training are confounded, and only one large model shows the effect.

No comparison to other incoherence-inducing perturbations (random noise, high temperature, adversarial context, repetition penalties, irrelevant text) is provided, so it is unclear whether the phenomenon is specific to activation steering or general self-repair after off-topic generation. The prefilling control actually shows restarts can be elicited text-conditionally in an unsteered model, undermining the 'endogenous' framing.

The metric is circular for the ablation claim: the judge segments attempts only on explicit restart phrases, and many of the 26 ablated latents are discourse/repair features (e.g., 'Expressions of dismay or realizing mistake', 'Sarcastic backtracking', 'The assistant needs to correct or clarify'). Ablating them may simply reduce the model's ability to emit correction language rather than impair an internal detection/resistance mechanism.

Mechanistic evidence is weak and confounded. The contrastive search yields a heterogeneous set with unreliable auto labels, about half showing negative effect sizes; ablating both positive- and negative-d subsets reduces ESR, which is inconsistent with a clean off-topic detector. The held-out-prompt ablation is underpowered (239 trials; 5.0% vs. 2.9-3.8% with overlapping CIs), and no cross-layer/circuit-level evidence is provided.

Effect sizes are very small and robustness is limited. The main ablation reduces ESR from 3.8% to 2.8% (1.0 percentage point); held-out differences are not statistically reliable. Cross-judge validation deliberately oversamples multi-attempt responses, so absolute ESR rates are not population estimates. Post hoc layer selection (e.g., steering Llama-3.3-70B at layer 33 despite SAE training at layer 50, selecting layer 22 for Gemma-2-27B based on higher ESR) may bias results.

The matched-prefix experiment does not establish sustained internal resistance. The residual advantage of natural post-correction text over a length-matched on-topic prefix could reflect richer or more effective text conditioning, not active suppression of steering. The continuation scores (8.7/30.4/54.5) come from a different simple relevance judge, not the validated 0-100 judge, and lack human validation.

Meta-prompting and fine-tuning results are mostly behavioral imitation: the meta-prompt explicitly instructs the model to self-correct, and fine-tuning trains on synthetic self-correction examples with loss masking; success rate remains flat. These do not provide strong evidence for enhancing an internal resistance mechanism.

Reproducibility and presentation issues: reliance on the proprietary Goodfire Ember API and auto-generated SAE labels; the abstract's code link appears incomplete; several references have inconsistent years; some tables/figures are truncated or missing detail (e.g., Table 4 held-out results, judge prompts with literal braces); no clear dataset/artifact release statement.

Significance is limited by the exploratory and largely negative/inconclusive findings. The paper does not deliver a robust mechanistic account or a generally useful intervention; safety implications remain speculative, with no tests on safety-relevant steering (harmful content, honesty, evaluation awareness).

strengths: The paper characterizes a genuinely interesting and under-explored phenomenon: mid-generation recovery from task-misaligned activation steering. The framing of Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR) and the explicit dissociation into detection vs. sustained-resistance components is a conceptually useful contribution.

The experimental methodology is unusually well-controlled for an exploratory interpretability study. The authors run a no-steering baseline (0% multi-attempt across 7,892 trials), a prefilling control, a length-matched-prefix experiment, a frequency/magnitude-matched random-latent ablation, a held-out prompt validation (5.0% baseline, 30–45% reduction under ablation), and a cross-judge panel of five models from different providers. These controls substantially strengthen the core claims.

The generalization check beyond SAE-derived directions (Wikipedia-derived contrastive vectors yielding 3.6% ESR vs. 3.8% SAE baseline, with a non-significant two-proportion test) is a valuable robustness result that rules out SAE-specific artifacts.

The paper is notably honest about its limitations and resists overclaiming: the terminology was revised from 'off-topic detectors' to 'self-correction-associated latents', the heterogeneous effect sizes (half with negative d) are disclosed, the unreliable holistic judge is documented rather than hidden, and post-hoc layer selection is flagged as a potential bias. This is exemplary treatment of limitations.
Reproducibility is good: code is released, judge prompts are fully provided, the full prompt set is listed, and fine-tuning hyperparameters are documented.

The deliberate-enhancement results (meta-prompting giving a 4.3x multi-attempt increase, fine-tuning inducing restarts) provide convergent evidence that the phenomenon is a manipulable behavioral lever rather than a measurement artifact.
weaknesses: The headline effect sizes are very small (3.8% ESR for Llama-3.3-70B, <1% for all other models), and the central causal result is a modest 25% relative reduction in multi-attempt rate from ablating 26 latents. This limits the practical significance and makes some secondary comparisons fragile.

The mechanistic story is incomplete and somewhat muddy. The 26 latents are a heterogeneous set, roughly half showing the opposite activation pattern, and both positive- and negative-d subsets reduce ESR comparably — which the authors admit is inconsistent with a clean 'detector' reading. The paper stops short of a circuit-level account, so the 'mechanistic identification' contribution is weaker than the contribution list implies.

The paper's own prefilling control undercuts the 'endogenous' framing: the restart event is shown to be largely text-conditioned and reproduces more often and more successfully without active steering. What remains 'endogenous' is only the residual post-correction quality, of which roughly half is attributed to ordinary autoregressive conditioning, leaving a modest unexplained remainder that the authors cannot cleanly attribute.

The cross-model comparison cannot disentangle scale, architecture, and training, and only a single model exhibits substantial ESR. This makes broad claims about 'larger models resisting steering' weakly supported (the related-work citation to Ali et al. is suggestive, not confirmatory).
The improvement-rate statistics for smaller models rest on very few episodes (e.g., n=5 for Gemma-2-2B), which the authors acknowledge but still report in figures, risking misinterpretation.

The fine-tuning experiment is a single recipe (LoRA on Llama-3.1-8B, one synthetic generator, one masking scheme, no training under active steering), so the dissociation between behavioral imitation and effective correction is informative but not generalizable.
Layer selection for steering was partly post-hoc (selecting the layer producing the most detectable ESR), which the authors acknowledge could bias results and complicates cross-model comparability.
